issues.description: The manuscript repeatedly treats cross-lagged associations from an autoregressive cross-lagged panel model as evidence of causation. Standard CLPMs do not identify causal effects because they do not adequately separate stable between-person differences from within-person change, and remain vulnerable to omitted time-varying confounds and reverse causation. The wording overstates what the design can support.
issues.quote: We used cross-lagged path analysis to infer causal associations between SDO, RWA and willingness to sacrifice for the environment.

issues.description: The discussion converts longitudinal associations into causal conclusions about motivation and psychological mechanisms. This is not justified by the observational design, especially given the absence of randomization, experimental manipulation, or stronger longitudinal models such as RI-CLPM or panel G-methods.
issues.quote: These results suggest that there is a causal pathway from ideological attitudes to environmentalism. The motivation to exploit the environment comes primarily from the desire for dominance, and to a lesser extent from the desire to submit to authority.

issues.description: The authors infer that SDO is 'foundational' for environmental attitudes from panel associations. This is a strong mechanistic causal interpretation not supported by the model used.
issues.quote: With our findings of a temporal connection between SDO and environmentalism, this strengthens our confidence in SDO having a causal effect on environmental attitudes, and perhaps even being foundational for these attitudes.

issues.description: The use of a traditional stationary CLPM for highly stable constructs (autoregressive paths .79, .95, .83) is problematic because the model likely conflates stable between-person differences with within-person dynamics. For trait-like ideological variables, a random-intercept cross-lagged panel model or similar approach is generally more appropriate.
issues.quote: The autoregressive paths for both SDO (B = .79... ) and RWA (B = .95... ) were similarly stable over time.

issues.description: The authors constrain all cross-lagged effects to be equal across all waves because they are 'more interested in the overall and comparative effects'. This is a substantive assumption that can distort estimates if effects differ over time. No formal comparison with less constrained alternatives is reported, and the equal-parameters assumption is not empirically justified.
issues.quote: Finally, we constrained the cross-lagged associations between the constructs to be the same in each measurement point. We imposed this stationary cross-lagged model because we were more interested in the overall and comparative effects...

issues.description: The description of invariance testing is incomplete and conceptually confused. The manuscript states that 'means (intercepts) of the factors' were constrained, then glosses this as making 'latent means' invariant. In longitudinal CFA, scalar invariance concerns item intercepts/thresholds, not factor means. Constraining latent means equal across time is a different assumption and may be inappropriate if there is mean change. No staged invariance testing or model comparisons are reported.
issues.quote: Next, we constrained the means (intercepts) of the factors to equality. Put concretely, this made the latent means of the three constructs invariance from Time 1 to Time 5.

issues.description: The manuscript does not report fit statistics, model comparisons, or decision criteria for the longitudinal measurement invariance constraints. Without evidence of configural/metric/scalar invariance, the meaning of latent variables and cross-time comparisons is uncertain.
issues.quote: We started by constraining the factor loadings of our latent variables to equality... Next, we constrained the means (intercepts) of the factors to equality... We also constrained to equality the residual variance for the same item over time...

issues.description: One RWA item was missing at Time 2, creating a different indicator set across waves. This complicates longitudinal invariance and comparability. The manuscript does not explain how the absent indicator was handled in the latent measurement model or whether partial invariance was used.
issues.quote: The item “Some of the best people in our country are those who are challenging our government, criticizing religion, and ignoring the “normal way” things are supposed to be done”, was not assessed at time two, but included in all other time points.

issues.description: A five-wave longitudinal analysis requires explicit reporting of retention at each wave, attrition patterns, and whether attrition was selective on key variables. Referring readers to a website is insufficient for evaluating bias and replicability.
issues.quote: Full details about the sample, including the procedure, retention, and demographics of participants, are available on the NZAVS website.

issues.description: There is no analysis of whether dropout across five years was associated with SDO, RWA, environmentalism, or demographics. FIML addresses missingness under MAR but does not resolve attrition bias if missingness depends on unobserved variables or poorly modeled observed predictors.
issues.quote: Missing data were imputed using FIML.

issues.description: FIML is not an imputation procedure. Describing it as 'imputed using FIML' is inaccurate and suggests potential confusion about the missing-data method used.
issues.quote: Missing data were imputed using FIML.

issues.description: The study claims to assess 'environmentalism' broadly, but operationalizes it narrowly as willingness to make personal sacrifices. This captures one behavioral intention dimension and may be influenced by financial constraints, lifestyle flexibility, political efficacy, or social desirability, rather than general environmental concern or behavior. The broad theoretical claims exceed the measure.
issues.quote: Environmentalism was measured as individual’s willingness to make sacrifices for the environment.

issues.description: The title, abstract, and discussion frequently discuss climate change, climate mitigation, and climate denial, but the measured outcome is a generic willingness-to-sacrifice-for-the-environment scale. This is not equivalent to climate change beliefs, denial, or support for climate policy.
issues.quote: We examine the longitudinal influence of SDO and RWA on people’s willingness to change their behaviour to benefit the environment...

issues.description: The manuscript oscillates between 'environmentalism,' 'pro-environmental attitudes,' 'willingness to change behaviour,' and climate change denial/mitigation. These are distinct constructs. The conclusions about climate change are not tightly linked to the specific measured variable.
issues.quote: While climate change is arguably the biggest environmental problem of our time... Our findings therefore highlight Social Dominant’s way of thinking as having the potential to exacerbate environmental inequality...

issues.description: The authors acknowledge reduced reliability for short SDO and RWA scales, but do not discuss the consequences for attenuation, measurement error, or comparability to prior work. Reliabilities around .69 and .70 are borderline and particularly consequential in longitudinal modeling.
issues.quote: Reliabilities for SDO and RWA were poorer than is typically the case when the full scales are used, but are consistent with expectations based on previous research using short measures [31].

issues.description: Regression/path estimates are reported with 'SD' rather than standard errors. In this context the reported quantities are clearly standard errors, not standard deviations. This is a statistical reporting error.

The authors infer that one correlation is stronger than another because their confidence intervals do not overlap. This is not the correct test for comparing dependent correlations sharing a variable, and can be misleading.
issues.quote: Of note here is that the zero-order correlation between SDO and environmentalism was stronger than the correlation for RWA, as indicated by the non-overlapping confidence interval.

issues.description: The chi-square difference/statistic is repeatedly reported without the chi-square symbol, producing ambiguous or incorrect statistical notation.
issues.quote: We found that our original model provides significantly better fit to the data 2(1) = 50.98, p < .001

issues.description: The reported chi-square difference comparing the SDO→RWA and RWA→SDO lagged effects is extraordinarily large relative to the tiny parameter estimates (.02 vs -.001) and sample size, suggesting a reporting or calculation error. Such a value is not credible without explanation.
issues.quote: These lagged effects were also statistically different (2(1) = 15,389.13, p < .001)

issues.description: The manuscript states that the 'traditional Wald test' was not possible due to constraints, but then conducts an equivalent nested-model equality test. The rationale is unclear and internally inconsistent; Mplus generally allows parameter constraints and Wald tests in such contexts.
issues.quote: Due to the nature of the analysis and the constraints placed on the model, the traditional Wald test to confirm that SDO is a statistically stronger predictor than RWA is not possible. Instead, we imposed similar constraints on the model as in the Wald test...

issues.description: The model is accepted despite poor CFI (.86), on the grounds that RMSEA and SRMR are acceptable and chi-square is affected by complexity. This selective emphasis is questionable, especially given the very complex model and substantial misfit by CFI. Poor fit raises concern about structural estimates under heavy constraints.
issues.quote: Overall, model fit was poorer for those indices affected by model complexity (e.g. χ2(2279) = 36511.73, p < .001, CFI = .86), however those less influenced by complexity pointed to good fit... therefore the model was accepted.

issues.description: Key model details are missing or inaccessible: Figure 1 is referenced but not provided here, standardized estimates are relegated to supplement, and there is no complete table of all constrained and unconstrained parameters, residual covariances, or wave-specific standardized effects in the main text.
issues.quote: Figure 1. Unstandardized parameters assessing the association between SDO, RWA, and willingness to sacrifice for the environment (WILL).

issues.description: The analysis code is not available during review, undermining reproducibility and evaluation of model specification.
issues.quote: A copy of the Mplus syntax used will be available on the NZAVS website upon acceptance of the manuscript.

issues.description: No preregistration, registered analysis plan, or indication of confirmatory versus exploratory modeling decisions is reported. Given multiple possible longitudinal specifications and substantial constraints, undisclosed analytic flexibility is a concern.
issues.quote: We tested the reciprocal influences between the constructs with a stationary cross-lagged model where all parameters are set as time-invariant.

issues.description: The decision to use p < .01 because of large sample size is ad hoc and does not address the more relevant issues of effect size interpretation, model uncertainty, multiple comparisons, or potential misspecification. It appears as an unregistered researcher degree of freedom.
issues.quote: Because of the large sample size of this dataset, we adopted a conservative p-value threshold of p < .01 to indicate significance of findings

issues.description: Although significance is emphasized, there is little interpretation of the practical magnitude of the cross-lagged effects, several of which are very small in unstandardized terms (e.g., RWA→environmentalism B = -.02). The manuscript does not contextualize whether these changes are substantively meaningful.

No time-invariant or time-varying covariates are included, despite obvious confounders such as political orientation, education, income, age, ethnicity, religiosity, and region that may affect both ideology and willingness to sacrifice. Omitting plausible confounds undermines causal interpretation and may bias cross-lagged paths.
issues.quote: The model thus included three latent variables across five measurement points, where each variable within a time point was set to predict each variable in the subsequent time point.

issues.description: The paper only briefly acknowledges third variables in the discussion, but does not incorporate or test them. Time-varying societal events, economic shocks, climate events, or political changes over 2009–2013 could induce associations among the variables.
issues.quote: Given the bidirectionality of our findings, a possible alternative explanation is that the relationship between ideology and environmentalism across time is explained by a third variable.

issues.description: The discussion states that the results are 'highly generalisable' to New Zealand, but the sample composition is heavily Pākehā and female, and no discussion of weighting, nonresponse adjustment, or representativeness over retained waves is provided. Generalizability is stronger than warranted.
issues.quote: Our research uses a nationally representative sample, meaning that our results are highly generalisable, at least to the New Zealand population.

issues.description: The paper makes broad claims about social dominance, environmentalism, and climate communication without adequately limiting them to the New Zealand sociopolitical context. Yet the authors themselves note that the relation between SDO and RWA may be context-dependent in New Zealand.
issues.quote: Because we found that RWA predicts SDO over time, but SDO does not predict RWA, this suggests that New Zealander’s are socialized into authoritarianism to a greater extent than social dominance.

issues.description: The conclusion reduces RWA to 'the desire to submit to authority and tradition,' while the literature reviewed in the manuscript itself notes multidimensionality (submission, aggression, conventionalism/tradition) and mixed associations of dimensions with environmentalism. Using a brief general RWA measure precludes such specific mechanism claims.
issues.quote: This result indicates that the desire to dominate leads to lower environmentalism in the future, which is influenced to a lesser extent by the desire to submit to authority and tradition.

issues.description: The abstract and discussion imply that findings identify a motivation to exploit the environment stemming from desire for dominance over nature or other groups. The study does not measure dominance-over-nature beliefs, anthropocentrism, hierarchy enforcement motives, or any mediating mechanism.
issues.quote: These findings suggest that the motivation to exploit the environment comes primarily from the desire for dominance...

issues.description: The manuscript calls the NZAVS a 'national probability sample' and 'nationally representative' but does not document the sampling frame, recruitment, response rate, weighting, or whether representativeness pertains to baseline only or retained panel. This creates tension between strong representativeness claims and missing details.
issues.quote: We used data from the New Zealand Attitudes and Values Study [26], a nationally representative, longitudinal study...

issues.description: Only Time 1 descriptive statistics are reported, despite a five-wave analysis and claims about stability and longitudinal change. Means, SDs, reliabilities, and correlations by wave are needed to evaluate trends, invariance assumptions, and possible period effects.
issues.quote: Table 1 presents the descriptive statistics and correlations between our variables at Time 1.

issues.description: The paper does not state which items were reverse-scored, whether parceling was used, whether item residuals were allowed to correlate across time, or how ordinal Likert responses were treated (continuous vs categorical). These choices materially affect SEM estimates.
issues.quote: Participants rated the extent to which they agreed with each item on 7-point Likert scales...

issues.description: All items are Likert-type with 7 response options, including a 2-item outcome with definite/maybe/yes anchors. The manuscript does not justify treating these as continuous nor specify the estimator used in Mplus. This omission matters because estimation and fit indices differ for categorical indicators.
issues.quote: Participants responded on a scale from 1 (definitely no) to 7 (definitely yes), with a midpoint of 4 (maybe).

issues.description: The SEM estimator (e.g., MLR, MLM, WLSMV) is not specified, preventing evaluation of standard errors, chi-square tests, and treatment of non-normality/ordinal indicators.
issues.quote: The autoregressive cross-lagged panel model allows examination of reciprocal influences among the three variables and was conducted in Mplus (version 7.3 [29]).

issues.description: Environmentalism is modeled as a latent construct with only two items. Two-indicator latent variables are weakly identified without strong assumptions, and can be sensitive to equality constraints and residual specifications. The manuscript provides no information on how identification was achieved.
issues.quote: Environmentalism was measured as individual’s willingness to make sacrifices for the environment... two items... The model thus included three latent variables across five measurement points

issues.description: The introduction appropriately notes that one should be cautious about directional claims and that environmentalism may also predict ideology, yet the discussion and conclusion nevertheless claim ideology causes environmentalism and interpret motivational mechanisms unambiguously.
issues.quote: This would mean that environmentalism drives ideology... we may find that environmentalism also predicts changes in ideology.
